newsitem.title: UK: Serbian opposition leader urges restored monarchy.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition leader urges restored monarchy.

text.p: A prominent Serbian opposition leader called on Wednesday for the restoration of the monarchy in his homeland, saying Crown Prince Alexander should take up the throne.

Vuk Draskovic of Serbia's Zajedno (Together) coalition said Alexander, who lives in exile in London, could play a similar role to King Juan Carlos of Spain, who smoothed his country's path to democracy after years of dictatorship.
Draskovic, who with fellow Zajedno leaders Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic was meeting Crown Prince Alexander on Wednesday, said all Serbia was shamed by the royal heir's continued exile.
"Serbia needs today our Serbian Juan Carlos and we have him in this city," Draskovic told reporters.
"That is shame on us, all of us in Serbia, that he has still the status of a refugee, he still has no Serbian citizenship and his private property is in the hands of Communist rulers."
Draskovic, a black-bearded nationalist whose views on the monarchy are not shared by all his fellow coalition members, said the restoration of Alexander must be decided by the Serbian people.
Crown Prince Alexander was born in 1945 at Claridges Hotel in London, where he will receive Draskovic and his fellow coalition members. He has declared himself ready to take up the throne.

As the heir to the Karadjordje throne must be born on Yugoslav soil, the British government, at the request of Alexander's father King Peter, deemed a suite in the hotel to be Yugoslav territory for a day.
But that same year, Yugoslavia's wartime leader Josip Broz Tito abolished the monarchy -- then known as the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.
Alexander, who has visited his homeland on three occasions, is the great-great-grandson of Queen Victoria and related to many of the crowned heads of Europe.

The Zajedno coalition leaders, fresh from the success of their three-month campaign of street demonstrations in Belgrade against the annulment of local election results, appealed to the West to support them now that they have won some power.
They said that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was applying "internal sanctions" by withholding government funds from municipalities won by the opposition.

Speaking after talks with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, the three leaders said they were ready to initiate dialogue on political and electoral reforms with Milosevic, as suggested by Western powers.
Pesic said that if the government did not respond to Zajedno's offer of dialogue, the opposition would call its supporters out on the streets again.
Rifkind said: "The British government strongly supports the process of dialogue...We will be urging President Milosevic to respond."
Britain is keen that all shades of political opinion are allowed access to the media in Serbia, where state broadcasters ignored the weeks of mass street protests against Milosevic.
The Zajedno leaders said that Serbia now needed speedy political and economic reforms.
"The protests have already shown that the majority are in favour of changes, but we need support from the outside world," said Djindjic, newly elected as mayor of Belgrade.
